quotes.text: You tell the waiter what you want from the menu and the plate comes back to your table. The menu is the agreement, and the waiter is the interface that carries your order between the two sides.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: A memorable everyday analogy that makes the abstract idea of an API instantly graspable.

quotes.text: A safe method doesn't change anything on the server, so sending it twice costs nothing. An idempotent method gives the same result whether you send it once or five times.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Clear definition of safe and idempotent methods, the key to understanding why retries can create duplicates.

quotes.text: A four hundred one means your sign in didn't take, and a four hundred and three means your sign in worked, but your account is missing the permission you need.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Practical distinction between authentication and authorization errors that saves real troubleshooting time.

quotes.text: A stolen API key can be reused for as long as it stays valid, which might be forever. A stolen bearer token is short lived by design, so it stops working on its own and gives you a window to cut access off.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Explains concisely why token-based authentication is safer than static API keys.

quotes.text: The connectors you click in Power Automate are Rest calls wearing a friendly face. When you drag in an action and fill out a few boxes, the connector builds the request for you.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Connects the theory directly to the low-code tools Microsoft 365 users already work with.

takeaways: A REST API call is one program asking another for something using an address, an HTTP verb, headers with proof of identity, and a response that starts with a status code.
Knowing which methods are safe or idempotent and what codes like 401, 403 and 429 mean turns failed flows from noise into problems you can fix.
The term REST comes from Roy Fielding's 2000 dissertation about the web's architecture, and most APIs called RESTful today only loosely follow it.
hook: Power Automate, Copilot Studio and Microsoft Graph all run on REST APIs, yet most users have never learned what happens behind a connector. This episode is for makers, admins and anyone troubleshooting flows who wants a plain-language explanation of requests, verbs, status codes, JSON and tokens. You will be able to read an API call and understand exactly what comes back.
